letters.name: A
letters.memoryTrick: A sounds like the 'a' in 'father' — just open your mouth and say 'ah!' It stays clean and open in every Tagalog word.

letters.name: Ba
letters.memoryTrick: B sounds just like English 'b' in 'ball' — press your lips together and release. It is never silent in Tagalog.

letters.name: Ca
letters.memoryTrick: In Filipino, C usually sounds like 'k' as in 'cat', or sometimes 's' as in 'city'. It appears almost exclusively in Spanish and English loanwords.

letters.name: Da
letters.memoryTrick: D sounds just like English 'd' in 'dog' — touch the tip of your tongue to the roof of your mouth right behind your teeth.

letters.name: E
letters.memoryTrick: E sounds like the 'e' in 'bed' — keep it short and crisp. In some words it can stretch slightly longer, but never like the English 'ee' in 'see'.

letters.name: Fa
letters.memoryTrick: F sounds exactly like English 'f' in 'fish' — top teeth on bottom lip, blow air through. Used mainly in loanwords like 'Filipino' and 'family'.

letters.name: Ga
letters.memoryTrick: G always has the hard 'g' sound as in 'go' or 'garden' — never soft like 'giraffe'. It's a sturdy, voiced sound made at the back of your mouth.

letters.name: Ha
letters.memoryTrick: H sounds like English 'h' in 'hat' — just a gentle breath of air. It is never silent in Tagalog; always pronounce it clearly.

letters.name: I
letters.memoryTrick: I sounds like 'ee' in 'see' — a long, clean vowel made with your tongue high and your lips spread wide.

letters.name: Ja
letters.memoryTrick: J can sound like Spanish 'j' (an English 'h' as in 'José') or like English 'j' in 'jam' for newer loanwords. The iconic Filipino 'jeep' uses the English-style sound.

letters.name: Ka
letters.memoryTrick: K sounds like English 'k' in 'kite' — crisp and quick with no puff of air. In Tagalog, K does a lot of work, appearing in many everyday words.

letters.name: La
letters.memoryTrick: L sounds like English 'l' in 'love' — let your tongue tip tap the roof of your mouth right behind your teeth. Keep it light; it's never the dark 'l' of English 'ball'.

letters.name: Ma
letters.memoryTrick: M sounds exactly like English 'm' in 'mom' — press your lips together and hum it out through your nose. One of the most common starting sounds in Tagalog.

letters.name: Na
letters.memoryTrick: N sounds like English 'n' in 'nose' — tongue tip to the roof of your mouth, air through your nose. Don't confuse it with the 'ng' sound, which is a separate letter in Filipino!

letters.name: Enye
letters.memoryTrick: Ñ (enye) sounds like 'ny' in 'canyon' — it's the same letter as Spanish 'ñ'. Think of words like 'piña' (pineapple) and 'niño' (boy). Press your tongue flat against the roof of your mouth.

letters.name: Nga
letters.memoryTrick: Ng sounds like 'ng' in 'sing' — but in Filipino, it can start a word! Try saying 'sing-along' and then drop the 'si' to get 'ngalong'. Words like 'ngipin' (tooth) and 'ngayon' (now) begin with this sound.

letters.name: O
letters.memoryTrick: O sounds like 'o' in 'open' — round your lips and let the sound out cleanly. It is never a diphthong like the English 'oh'.

letters.name: Pa
letters.memoryTrick: P sounds like English 'p' in 'pot' — but without the puff of air. Hold your hand in front of your mouth; you should feel very little breath when you say Tagalog 'p'.

letters.name: Qa
letters.memoryTrick: Q always pairs with U in Filipino and sounds like 'k' as in 'king'. It appears only in loanwords like 'quiz' and 'queen'. Think of it as a fancy K!

letters.name: Ra
letters.memoryTrick: R is a light tap of the tongue, like the 'tt' in the American pronunciation of 'butter'. It is never the rolling R of Spanish — just one quick tap above your teeth.

letters.name: Sa
letters.memoryTrick: S sounds like English 's' in 'sun' — a smooth hissing sound. It is always unvoiced; it never buzzes like a 'z' as it sometimes does in English.

letters.name: Ta
letters.memoryTrick: T sounds like English 't' in 'top' — but without the puff of air. Place the tip of your tongue right behind your upper teeth and release cleanly.

letters.name: U
letters.memoryTrick: U sounds like 'oo' in 'food' — purse your lips and let it hum. It is a pure vowel, never sliding into a 'y' sound at the end like English 'you'.

letters.name: Va
letters.memoryTrick: V sounds like English 'v' in 'van' — top teeth on bottom lip. Used in loanwords; some Filipino speakers pronounce it the same as 'b', so don't be surprised if you hear both.

letters.name: Wa
letters.memoryTrick: W sounds like English 'w' in 'water' — round your lips and glide into the next vowel. It appears in several common Tagalog words like 'wala' (none) and 'walo' (eight).

letters.name: Xa
letters.memoryTrick: X usually sounds like 'ks' as in 'box', or sometimes 'h' (as in Spanish 'Mexico'). It appears only in loanwords — 'x-ray' and 'xylophone' are the most common.

letters.name: Ya
letters.memoryTrick: Y sounds like 'y' in 'yes' — a quick glide at the start of a syllable. It's a consonant at the start of words like 'yelo' (ice) and 'yakap' (hug).

letters.name: Za
letters.memoryTrick: Z sounds like English 'z' in 'zebra' — a buzzing 's' with your vocal cords vibrating. Used in loanwords; some speakers pronounce it like 's', so you may hear both versions.
